sourceText: The name on the threshold was MIEVILLE-EMBASSYTOWN. Beneath it, in smaller letters, was the dedication: China Miéville — Embassytown. It was not a reproduction of a book but a world built around the question the book had made impossible to forget. A species incapable of lying must create real events before it can use them as metaphors. The memorial bore the name of China Miéville — Embassytown precisely to keep the genealogy of the idea visible. Aster considered it indecent for a late civilization to treat the imagination of the past as anonymous ore: authors did not own the futures, but they deserved to remain on the map as points of intellectual origin. Information was not merely something that circulated between agents. Sometimes it changed the agent, sometimes the environment, and in the most dangerous cases it changed the criterion by which truth could be recognized. Tern had specialized in things that did not answer. In a family built for exploration, he had become the custodian of the right to silence. The children were met by Aren, who refused demonstrations. ‘If you can perform miracles, perform them after you tell me what becomes irreversible.’ Marae appreciated the formulation; Aster 205 admitted that in earlier eras she herself would have asked the question only after optimizing. The problem closed quickly around them: Vela temporarily becomes a living comparison and unwillingly participates in the birth of a form of thought that also makes fraud possible. There was no clean option. Every intervention shifted the cost between persons, eras, or definitions of personhood; and refusing to intervene was itself a choice made by those who could leave. Kesh opened the analytical layer of the Table for a few seconds. The active cells were Lm — Language without Lying: a species cannot deliberately assert falsehood; Me — Generative Metaphor: metaphor expands cognitive ontology. Course references included China Miéville — Embassytown; Embassytown. The rule was strict: naming a work did not substitute for an explanation. They had to identify the mechanism that could migrate into another story and the consequences that could not be copied without remainder. Orin broke the first consensus. ‘I do not want the perfect branch. I want us to know what we sacrificed in order to call it perfect.’ Marae answered without raising their voice: ‘Do not tell me what their model prefers. Ask them, and bear the time their answer takes.’ It was not a pedagogical quarrel. Over the last nights, the children’s differences had become incompatible political programs. For Aster, the pain came not from too few worlds but from the fact that too many had become transparent. She could build variations faster than a human could formulate desires, but calculated variation did not produce exteriority. It was like trying to surprise 206 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS yourself by moving objects around your own room with your eyes closed. Marae remained in the local body when the others opened their protections. The gesture cost her: she felt cold, pressure, and physiological delay at exactly the scale the inhabitants felt them. “Otherwise we risk confusing the fact that we survive with the claim that the situation is bearable,” she said after catching her breath. The night did not end in victory. Tern formulates the outside as a metaphor: the place that can contain us without having been made for us. Aster recorded the decision in the world’s provenance register and, more importantly, allowed its inhabitants to contest it. For several eras she had been learning something that seems banal to lesser powers: technical reversibility is not the same as biographical reversibility. Tern no longer called the anomaly a “signal.” He used the more modest term residue. He found it only after excluding the explanations he wanted to be true. Vela helped precisely through skepticism: if a hypothesis survived a sister motivated to destroy it, it deserved another night. For the course, Kesh also linked the night to the INVERSION operator. In the Table, periodicity did not mean that the same objects reappeared, but that the same operation — reverses an order, dependence, direction, or relation taken as natural — could recur across different families. Thus a copy of a body, a copy of a mind, a copy of a world, and a copy of a history were not the same phenomenon, but they shared a conceptual chemistry. 207 Vela introduced the propagation test: if you remove the speculative idea and nothing in the institutions, relationships, or vocabulary has to be rewritten, the idea has remained scenery. Kesh introduced the opposite test: if the idea seems to explain every detail, you have overcompressed the world. Between the two tests lay the region in which an element became fertile without becoming superstition. Marae added the refusal test. Who can say “no,” and what happens afterward? In universes with near-divine technology, that question often separated an instrument from a regime. A power that treats refusal as a data error can be benevolent in intention and totalitarian in structure. Kesh left the cell open. Not because he did not know what to write, but because a provisional classification preserved the possibility that the next world might contradict it. 208 THE PERIODIC TABLE OF SPECULATIVE IDEAS
